[word/document.xml] Field Operations
[word/document.xml] 1.1 Roles and Crew Organization
[word/document.xml] 2. Instrument Transition Drills: Practice smooth, rapid instrument placement and retrieval from the central carrier tote during timed entry, staging, and exit drills.

[word/document.xml] 3. Rehearsal Run-Throughs: Conduct full-speed timed entry, positioning, brake-setting, brake-releasing, and exit drills during dress rehearsals on both synthetic turf and natural grass surfaces.

[word/document.xml] 4. Handshake & Communication Protocol: The student on the outer sideline edge acts as the primary caller ('Clear left', 'Approaching curb', 'Brakes locked', 'Brakes released'). Handlers maintain continuous verbal communication during moves.

-[word/document.xml] 5. High Wind Emergency Response: If sustained winds exceed 20 mph or sudden gusts threaten prop stability during a performance, student handlers maintain firm contact on the wooden base with all brakes locked. Parent pit crew members stationed along the sideline with Field Pass wristbands will step onto the field to provide perimeter stabilization as directed by band directors.
-[word/document.xml] 1.4 Ballasting System, Wing Retention Posts, and Double-Bagging Protocol
-[word/document.xml] To maintain vertical stability against outdoor wind shear while protecting stadium athletic turf, follow this exact ballasting standard:

-[word/document.xml] 1. Vertical Ballast Retention Posts: Each cart is equipped with two vertical 3/4-in. black iron pipe posts (18 inches tall) screwed into floor flanges through-bolted to the center of the left and right 1/2" plywood decking wings (see Appendix B, Stage 2).

-[word/document.xml] 2. Primary Ballast Standard (4–6 Bags, 60–90 lbs): Standard ballasting uses 4 to 6 15-lb heavy-duty sandbags with sewn-in handles (Index [13]). Stack 2 to 3 sandbags on the left wing and 2 to 3 sandbags on the right wing, looping the handles securely over the 3/4" vertical iron pipe posts. The vertical posts prevent sandbags from shifting, sliding off, or falling during cart movement or high winds.

-[word/document.xml] 3. Mandatory Double-Bagging (Rule 8.05): All 15-lb sandbags MUST utilize heavy-duty inner plastic liner insert bags (Index [14]) sealed securely inside the outer fabric sandbags. This dual-layer containment strictly satisfies the mandatory CBA competition anti-leakage rule.

-[word/document.xml] 4. High-Wind Reserve Ballast (70-lb Tube Sand): On severe high-wind days (sustained winds >15–20 mph), crew may add one or two 70-lb Sakrete traction tube sand bags (Index [15]) placed across the lower center frame joists. MANDATORY: Every 70-lb tube sandbag MUST be completely wrapped and sealed inside a thick contractor-grade garbage bag to satisfy the secondary containment rule before entering the stadium.

-[word/document.xml] CRITICAL TURF OPERATION & DOUBLE-BAGGING WARNING: Under no circumstances may unbagged or single-layer sandbags be brought onto any competition turf (see Section 1.5, Rule 8.05). In addition, do not exceed 100–140 lbs total ballast under normal conditions, as excessive weight causes casters to sink into artificial turf rubber infill, multiplying rolling friction and making carts sluggish for student handlers.

+[word/document.xml] 5. High Wind Emergency Response & Abort Protocol: If sustained winds exceed 20 mph or sudden gusts exceed 25 mph, rolling backdrops MUST NOT enter the performance field (strict safety NO-GO threshold). If severe gusts strike while props are already on the field, student handlers must immediately lock all four caster brakes, position themselves on the upwind side of the cart, and brace the lower 2x4 framing. At no time should students attempt to hold backdrops from the upper steel pipe rails or climb the frame. Designated parent volunteers with Field Pass wristbands (Rule 9.07) will step onto the field to provide perimeter stabilization or assist handlers in immediately tipping the props flat onto the turf if ordered by band directors.
+[word/document.xml] 1.4 Ballasting System, Tiered Wind Schedule, and Double-Bagging Protocol

+[word/document.xml] To maintain vertical stability against outdoor wind shear while strictly protecting stadium athletic turf from rutting and sand contamination, all backdrop props must adhere to this engineering ballasting standard and operational loading schedule.

+[word/document.xml] B. High-Wind Rear-Rail Ballast Leverage Optimization
+[word/document.xml] Because the 10 ft x 8 ft vertical upright steel frame sits on the front perimeter rail (A) of the cart base, the structure possesses an inherent tipping asymmetry:

+[word/document.xml] 1. Critical Failure Mode (Forward Tipping): When wind blows from the rear toward the front, the cart pivots about the front caster wheels. Because the 48-lb steel frame and vinyl banner sit directly above the front caster line, their deadweight provides zero restoring leverage. As a result, an unballasted prop tips forward at just 12.4 mph (11.2 mph at sea level).

+[word/document.xml] 2. The Rear-Rail Mechanical Advantage: The 3/4-in. wing pipe posts sit at mid-depth (22.25 in. from front), providing a restoring lever arm of 1.71 ft to the front casters. By contrast, placing supplemental sandbags along the rear 2x4 framing rail (A) behind the instrument tote increases the lever arm to 3.46 ft (41.5 in.)—more than double the mechanical leverage! Three 15-lb bags placed across the rear rail produce the overturning resistance of six bags stacked on the center posts, equalizing forward and backward tipping thresholds to 22.5 mph.

+[word/document.xml] 3. Turf Compaction Ceiling: Total supplemental ballast must never exceed 140 lbs (293 lbs total prop deadweight). Concentrating more than ~75 lbs per caster wheel causes casters to sink into artificial turf rubber infill, multiplying rolling drag and risking permanent turf depressions or track damage.
+[word/document.xml] C. Mandatory Double-Bagging Protocol (CBA Rule 8.05)

+[word/document.xml] All 15-lb sandbags MUST utilize heavy-duty inner plastic liner insert bags (Index [14]) sealed securely inside the outer fabric cordura bags. Under no circumstances may unbagged or single-layer sandbags be brought onto any competition turf. If an outer fabric bag abrades, splits, or suffers seam failure, the heavy-duty inner liner guarantees zero sand escapes onto the performance field.
+[word/document.xml] D. Emergency Reserve Protocol (70-lb Tube Sand)

+[word/document.xml] In the event that 15-lb handle sandbags are depleted or extreme wind gusts threaten during stationary staging, crew may deploy 1 to 2 70-lb Sakrete traction tube sand bags (Index [15]) positioned flat across the rear lumber framing rail. MANDATORY: Every 70-lb tube sandbag MUST be completely wrapped and sealed inside a thick contractor-grade garbage bag to satisfy the secondary containment rule before entering the stadium.

+[word/document.xml] CRITICAL TURF OPERATION & DOUBLE-BAGGING WARNING: Under no circumstances may unbagged or single-layer sandbags be brought onto any competition turf (see Section 1.5, Rule 8.05). In addition, do not exceed 135–140 lbs total ballast under any operational conditions, as excessive weight causes casters to sink into artificial turf rubber infill, multiplying rolling friction and making carts sluggish for student handlers.

[word/document.xml] Tools and equipment
[word/document.xml] Required workshop tools and fixtures:
[word/document.xml] • Miter saw or circular saw with wood framing blade

[word/document.xml] Before adhering tape or wrapping vinyl, use a fresh, sharp utility razor knife to make small, neat relief slits in the vinyl bleed wrap allowance to accommodate protruding frame hardware:

[word/document.xml] • Long edges (Vertical Uprights): Cut small slits directly aligned with the diagonal support strut attachment brackets (tension bands) on the left and right upright rails. These slits allow the strut brackets to protrude through the bleed wrap cleanly, preventing unsightly puckering, tenting, or bunching of the visible banner face.

[word/document.xml] • Bottom edge (Cart-Mounting Interface): Cut two small relief slits along the bottom rail bleed wrap corresponding to the base tension bands and mounting brackets that secure the upright frame to the wood cart base.
+[word/document.xml] Step 3.1: Cutting Engineered Wind Relief Slits

+[word/document.xml] To prevent violent wind flutter, reduce peak dynamic overturning impulses during stadium gusts, and protect greenhouse snap clamps from popping off under high wind loads, cut six (6) engineered inverted-U crescent wind relief flaps into the custom vinyl banner while it remains face-down on the cushioned moving blankets:

+[word/document.xml] • Mandatory Tear-Arrest Relief Holes: CRITICAL FABRICATION RULE: NEVER cut wind relief slits purely with a utility razor knife leaving sharp 90° corners. Sharp razor corners create extreme stress concentration factors (Kt ≥ 3.0) that will rapidly propagate into catastrophic tears across the entire banner during the first stadium wind gust. Before making any razor cuts, use a 3/8-in. (10 mm) rotary leather punch or clean gasket punch against a wooden backup block to punch two smooth, circular holes at the upper hinge corners of each planned flap.

+[word/document.xml] • Inverted "U" Crescent Flap Geometry: Each flap measures 8.0 in. wide with a 5.0 to 6.0 in. downward curved drop. The top 8.0-in. span between the two punched relief holes remains uncut to serve as a flexible vinyl hinge. Using a fresh utility razor knife, cut a smooth downward curve starting from the bottom of one hole, curving down 5 to 6 inches, and terminating cleanly into the bottom of the second hole.

+[word/document.xml] • Aerodynamic Function & Audience Appearance: Under calm conditions, gravity pulls the flap flush against the banner face. From audience stands 50 to 150 feet away, the narrow slit line is virtually invisible, preserving complete graphic visual continuity. Under forward or rear wind pressure, the flap swings open freely, venting dynamic pressure spikes and damping vortex-shedding flutter oscillations.

+[word/document.xml] • Upper-Venting Zone Layout (Row 1 & Row 2): Because overturning moment increases directly with height above the turf (M = F · y), venting pressure near the top of the prop is 2.5 times more effective at preventing tipping than venting near the bottom. Slits must be concentrated in the upper 40%–60% of the banner:

+[word/document.xml] - Row 1 (Upper Tier): Located 8.0 ft (96 in.) above the bottom rail (2.0 ft below top rail). Center three flaps across the width at X = 2.0 ft (24 in.), X = 4.0 ft (48 in. centerline), and X = 6.0 ft (72 in.) from the left outer edge.

+[word/document.xml] - Row 2 (Mid-Upper Tier): Located 5.5 ft (66 in.) above the bottom rail. Center three flaps across the width at X = 2.0 ft (24 in.), X = 4.0 ft (48 in. centerline), and X = 6.0 ft (72 in.) from the left outer edge.

+[word/document.xml] • Artwork & Graphic Clearance Rules: Before punching or cutting, inspect the front face of the custom printed artwork. Adjust flap centerlines horizontally by ±6 to 12 inches to place slits in solid background fields, skies, or low-contrast negative space. NEVER cut across student performer faces, school crests, band logos, or sharp typographic lettering.
